title: The Umayyad Mosque
hook: the great mosque of Damascus, built on a site holy for centuries, still has a shrine honoring Yahya (John the Baptist)

segments.voice: Yesterday: sakhrah, the rock under the dome in Jerusalem. Your line was a dome over the rock.

In the prayer hall of the great mosque of Damascus, among the carpets and the columns, stands a small domed shrine behind a grille. People stop at it. Some touch the grille. Some pray beside it. Christians come to it too. It honors a prophet the Qur'an calls Yahya, and Christians call John the Baptist. Tradition says his head is buried there. A shrine to John inside a mosque, in the old capital of the caliphs. Today: the Umayyad Mosque.

Start with the ground under it. The histories describe this site as holy before Islam: a temple in Roman times, and later a church dedicated to John the Baptist. Later histories report that after the Muslims came to Damascus, for a time Muslims and Christians both prayed on the site. Then the Umayyad caliph al-Walid, son of Abd al-Malik, built the great mosque here, reusing the old walls. So the mosque stands on layer upon layer of prayer. And it kept John. The Qur'an tells Yahya's story with warmth: "Peace on him the day he was born, and the day he dieth and the day he shall be raised alive!" Another layer looks forward. One of the mosque's minarets is called the Minaret of Jesus. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that Jesus son of Mary will descend near a white minaret east of Damascus, and tradition links that report to this tower. So one building holds a Roman past, a Christian past, a Muslim present, and a hope about the end of days. Then the courtyard, wide and open, and the gold mosaics of trees, rivers and houses on its walls, which some readers see as a picture of paradise. Old stone, many prayers, one place. Layers of holiness.

Bring the courtyard to mind: wide stone, open sky, pigeons, minarets above, and around it a very old city, home to families of more than one faith, that has lived through hard years. If you pray, ask God for peace on Damascus and its people, in your own words or in silence. If you don't, hold the city in mind with goodwill, one breath at a time.
Yahya, the Qur'an's name for John the Baptist: the prophet honored with a shrine inside the great mosque of Damascus, built on layer upon layer of older prayer. Today's word.
Your line: layers of holiness. One place, prayed in again and again. Day nine hundred five, done.

howItsDone: Worshipers at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus pray in its great hall and visit the shrine honoring Yahya (John the Baptist), which Christian visitors also come to.

chat.says: Why would a mosque in Damascus have a shrine to John the Baptist?
options: Muslims honor him as Yahya, a prophet; tradition says his head lies there.
Only Christians honor him; the shrine is kept just for their visits.
It was left over from the old church by mistake and is rarely visited.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an calls John the Baptist Yahya and greets him with peace; tradition says his head is buried in the shrine.
